key_terms.meaning: p<sub>m</sub> = w<sub>net</sub>/(v₁ − v₂); power = p<sub>m</sub>V<sub>s</sub>N/120 per cylinder (four-stroke)
[(h₁ − h₂) − (h₄ − h₃)]/(h₁ − h₄); pump work v<sub>f</sub>Δp
(h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁), h₄ = h₃; 1 TR = 3.517 kW

takeaways: Every air standard cycle is a fixed mass of ideal air in reversible processes; its efficiency depends only on the cycle's ratios, never on the fuel.
The Carnot cycle sets the limit but has a tiny work ratio and mean effective pressure, so no engine runs on it.
Otto, Diesel and Dual differ only in how heat goes in; at equal compression ratio and heat input Otto is the most efficient, at equal peak pressure Diesel is.
The Brayton efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio; the net work peaks at T₂ = T₄ = √(T₁T₃).
A perfect regenerator gives the Stirling cycle the Carnot efficiency; without one it falls far below.
In steam and refrigerant cycles every work and heat is an enthalpy difference read from tables; check whether each state is wet or superheated first.
Higher boiler pressure, higher superheat and lower condenser pressure all raise the Rankine efficiency by raising the mean temperature of heat addition or lowering that of rejection.
Reheat keeps the turbine exhaust dry; regeneration raises the efficiency by heating the feedwater with bled steam.
The vapour compression COP is (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁); it falls as the evaporator gets colder or the condenser hotter.
An absorption plant trades the compressor for an absorber, pump and generator driven by heat; its COP is below 1 but its input can be waste heat.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the p-v and T-s diagrams and the derivation of the air standard efficiency of the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles, a numerical problem on one of them with the mean effective pressure, and the comparison of the three cycles. Syllabi that include steam and refrigeration ask for a Rankine problem from steam tables and a vapour compression problem from refrigerant tables.

bank.q: With p-v and T-s diagrams, derive the air standard efficiency of the Otto cycle. Show how it changes with compression ratio, with values for r = 6, 8 and 10 (γ = 1.4), and explain why a petrol engine cannot simply use a very high compression ratio.
outline: Four processes on p-v and T-s
q<sub>in</sub> and q<sub>out</sub> at constant volume

answer.text: Assumptions: a fixed mass of air, an ideal gas with constant c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4; heat added and rejected from outside; all processes internally reversible. State 1 is the start of compression.

The four processes, drawn below: 1→2 isentropic compression; 2→3 heat addition at constant volume; 3→4 isentropic expansion; 4→1 heat rejection at constant volume. On p-v, 2→3 and 4→1 are vertical lines and 1→2, 3→4 are curves pv<sup>γ</sup> = constant. On T-s, 1→2 and 3→4 are vertical lines and 2→3, 4→1 are constant-volume curves that rise to the right.

svg.aria: Sketch of the Otto cycle: on p-v two isentropic curves joined by two vertical constant-volume lines; on T-s two vertical isentropic lines joined by two rising constant-volume curves.

answer.text: Compression ratio r = v₁/v₂. Because v₃ = v₂ and v₄ = v₁, the expansion ratio v₄/v₃ is also r.
Heat added and rejected per kg (constant volume, so q = c<sub>v</sub>ΔT):
answer.pre:
q<sub>in</sub>  = c<sub>v</sub>(T₃ − T₂)
q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁)
η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub> = 1 − (T₄ − T₁)/(T₃ − T₂)

answer.text: Isentropic relations: T₂/T₁ = (v₁/v₂)<sup>γ−1</sup> = r<sup>γ−1</sup> and T₃/T₄ = (v₄/v₃)<sup>γ−1</sup> = r<sup>γ−1</sup>. So T₂ = T₁r<sup>γ−1</sup> and T₃ = T₄r<sup>γ−1</sup>.
Substitute:
answer.pre:
T₃ − T₂ = r<sup>γ−1</sup>(T₄ − T₁)
η = 1 − (T₄ − T₁)/[r<sup>γ−1</sup>(T₄ − T₁)]
η<sub>Otto</sub> = 1 − 1/r<sup>γ−1</sup>

answer.text: The efficiency depends only on r and γ, not on the heat added or the starting temperature. Values with γ = 1.4:

Trend: η rises with r, quickly at first and then more slowly; going from r = 6 to 8 gains 5.3 points, from 8 to 10 only 3.7. On the T-s diagram, a higher r lifts state 2, so heat is added at a higher mean temperature while heat is still rejected along the same constant-volume line from state 4 down to state 1.

Why not a very high r: a petrol engine compresses a mixture of fuel and air. The temperature at the end of compression rises as r<sup>γ−1</sup>; above r of about 10 to 12 for ordinary petrol, part of the charge self-ignites before the flame from the spark reaches it. This knock gives sharp pressure waves that damage pistons and bearings. So the fuel's anti-knock quality, not thermodynamics, limits r. A diesel engine compresses only air and injects fuel at the end, so it can use r of 14 to 22.
Check with numbers: for r = 8, T₁ = 300 K and q<sub>in</sub> = 800 kJ/kg, the worked example gives T₄ = 785.0 K, q<sub>out</sub> = 348.2 kJ/kg and η = 451.8/800 = 0.565, the same as the formula.

bank.q: Derive the air standard efficiency of the Diesel cycle in terms of the compression ratio and cut-off ratio. Show that it is less than the Otto efficiency at the same compression ratio, and find both for r = 16 with r<sub>c</sub> = 2.
outline: q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₂), q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁)
T₂, T₃, T₄ in terms of T₁

answer.text: Processes: 1→2 isentropic compression; 2→3 heat addition at constant pressure; 3→4 isentropic expansion; 4→1 heat rejection at constant volume. On p-v, 2→3 is a horizontal line and 4→1 a vertical line; on T-s, 2→3 is a constant-pressure curve, flatter than the constant-volume curve 4→1.
Ratios: compression ratio r = v₁/v₂; cut-off ratio r<sub>c</sub> = v₃/v₂. Since p₂ = p₃, the ideal gas law gives T₃/T₂ = v₃/v₂ = r<sub>c</sub>.
Heat terms:
answer.pre:
q<sub>in</sub>  = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₂)   (constant pressure)
q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁)   (constant volume)
η = 1 − (T₄ − T₁)/[γ(T₃ − T₂)]

answer.text: Temperatures in terms of T₁:
answer.pre:
T₂ = T₁ r<sup>γ−1</sup>
T₃ = r<sub>c</sub> T₂ = T₁ r<sub>c</sub> r<sup>γ−1</sup>
T₄ = T₃ (v₃/v₄)<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₃ (r<sub>c</sub>/r)<sup>γ−1</sup>   (v₄ = v₁)
   = T₁ r<sub>c</sub> r<sup>γ−1</sup> r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ−1</sup>/r<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₁ r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup>

answer.text: Substitute:

Comparison with Otto: the Otto efficiency is 1 − 1/r<sup>γ−1</sup>. The Diesel formula multiplies 1/r<sup>γ−1</sup> by B = (r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> − 1)/[γ(r<sub>c</sub> − 1)]. For r<sub>c</sub> > 1, B > 1: the function r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> has slope γr<sub>c</sub><sup>γ−1</sup>, which is above γ for every r<sub>c</sub> > 1, so r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> − 1 grows faster than γ(r<sub>c</sub> − 1). Hence η<sub>Diesel</sub> < η<sub>Otto</sub> at the same r, and B → 1 (Diesel → Otto) as r<sub>c</sub> → 1.
Numbers for r = 16, r<sub>c</sub> = 2, γ = 1.4:

Physical reason, from the T-s diagram: with states 1 and 2 shared, the constant-pressure line 2→3 is flatter than a constant-volume line, so the Diesel cycle takes in heat over a larger entropy range at a lower mean temperature, and it rejects more heat along the longer constant-volume line 4→1.

Check: the Diesel worked example (r = 15, r<sub>c</sub> = 1.84) gave η = 457.8/748.2 = 0.612 from the heat balance and 0.612 from this formula. So the diesel engine is more efficient in practice only because it runs at a higher r than a petrol engine can.

bank.q: Explain the Rankine cycle with a layout and T-s diagram, write its efficiency in terms of enthalpies, and discuss the effect of boiler pressure, superheat temperature and condenser pressure on its efficiency and on the dryness of the turbine exhaust.
outline: η in enthalpies, pump work v<sub>f</sub>Δp
effect of each change with numbers

answer.text: Layout: the pump sends water from the condenser to the boiler at high pressure; the boiler heats, boils and superheats it; the steam expands in the turbine and drives the generator; the condenser turns the exhaust back into saturated water using cooling water. All four are steady-flow devices.

States: 1 turbine inlet (superheated steam), 2 turbine exit (usually wet), 3 condenser exit (saturated liquid), 4 pump exit (compressed liquid). Processes: 1→2 and 3→4 isentropic, 2→3 and 4→1 at constant pressure. The T-s diagram below is for steam at 40 bar and 400 °C with a condenser at 0.1 bar.

svg.aria: T-s diagram of the Rankine cycle at 40 bar, 400 °C and 0.1 bar, inside and around the water dome.

answer.text: Energy terms from the steady flow energy equation (kJ/kg):
answer.pre:
w<sub>T</sub> = h₁ − h₂        w<sub>P</sub> = h₄ − h₃ = v<sub>f</sub>(p₁ − p₃)
q<sub>in</sub> = h₁ − h₄       q<sub>out</sub> = h₂ − h₃
η = (w<sub>T</sub> − w<sub>P</sub>)/q<sub>in</sub>    SSC = 3600/(w<sub>T</sub> − w<sub>P</sub>) kg/kWh

answer.text: A clean way to reason about every change: write T<sub>m</sub> = q<sub>in</sub>/(s₁ − s₄), the mean temperature at which heat enters. Then η = 1 − T<sub>cond</sub>/T<sub>m</sub> (kelvin). For this plant T<sub>m</sub> = 3018.7/6.122 = 493 K and 1 − 318.96/493 = 0.353.
Effects, one change at a time from 40 bar, 400 °C, 0.1 bar (computed from steam tables):

Boiler pressure: a higher pressure raises the boiling temperature and so T<sub>m</sub>; η rises. But at the same steam temperature s₁ falls, so the isentropic expansion ends further inside the dome and the exhaust is wetter. Water droplets erode the last-stage blades.

Superheat: a higher steam temperature raises T<sub>m</sub> and also raises s₁, so the exhaust is drier. It is limited by the creep strength of superheater tubes and turbine materials, at about 540 to 600 °C in current plants.

Condenser pressure: a lower pressure lowers the temperature of heat rejection. The turbine work rises more than the heat input, so η rises; the exhaust is a little wetter, and the plant needs a good vacuum and cold cooling water.

Conclusion: plants raise the pressure for efficiency and combine it with high superheat and reheat to keep the exhaust dryness above about 0.88 to 0.90; regeneration then raises the efficiency further.

svg.aria: Ammonia-water absorption refrigerator: generator, condenser, valve, evaporator, absorber, pump and solution heat exchanger with heat flows.

answer.text: Refrigerant path: liquid ammonia from the condenser is throttled in the expansion valve to the evaporator pressure; it boils in the evaporator, taking heat Q<sub>E</sub> from the cold space. The low-pressure vapour goes to the absorber.

Solution path: in the absorber the ammonia vapour dissolves in weak solution coming from the generator, making strong solution. Absorption releases heat Q<sub>A</sub>, removed by cooling water, because a cool solution holds more ammonia. The pump lifts the strong solution to the high pressure, through the solution heat exchanger, where it is warmed by the hot weak solution returning, and into the generator.

In the generator, heat Q<sub>G</sub> from steam, hot water or exhaust drives ammonia vapour out of the solution. Some water vapour comes with it; the analyser and rectifier condense it so nearly dry ammonia goes to the condenser, where it condenses, rejecting Q<sub>C</sub>. The weak solution flows back through the heat exchanger and a pressure-reducing valve to the absorber.
The absorber, pump and generator together do the compressor's job. Raising the pressure of a liquid needs far less work than compressing a vapour, so the pump work W<sub>P</sub> is small.
Energy balance and COP:
answer.pre:
Q<sub>G</sub> + Q<sub>E</sub> + W<sub>P</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + Q<sub>A</sub>
COP = Q<sub>E</sub>/(Q<sub>G</sub> + W<sub>P</sub>) ≈ Q<sub>E</sub>/Q<sub>G</sub>

answer.text: Maximum COP: heat Q<sub>G</sub> enters at T<sub>G</sub>, Q<sub>E</sub> at T<sub>E</sub>, and Q<sub>C</sub> + Q<sub>A</sub> leaves at the ambient T<sub>0</sub>. A reversible plant is equivalent to a Carnot engine between T<sub>G</sub> and T<sub>0</sub> driving a Carnot refrigerator between T<sub>E</sub> and T<sub>0</sub>:
answer.pre:
W = Q<sub>G</sub>(1 − T<sub>0</sub>/T<sub>G</sub>)
Q<sub>E</sub> = W × T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>0</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>)
COP<sub>max</sub> = (1 − T<sub>0</sub>/T<sub>G</sub>) × T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>0</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>)

answer.text: Example: T<sub>G</sub> = 393.15 K, T<sub>0</sub> = 303.15 K, T<sub>E</sub> = 263.15 K gives 0.2289 × 6.579 = 1.51. A real single-stage plant reaches about 0.5 to 0.7.
Comparison:

head: Feature
Vapour compression
Vapour absorption
rows: heat at 80 to 180 °C, small pump work

answer.text: Conclusion: absorption wins where heat is free or cheap (waste heat, exhaust, solar) or electricity is short; compression wins where electricity is cheap and space is tight.

bank.q: Compare the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles (a) for the same compression ratio and heat input and (b) for the same maximum pressure and temperature, using T-s diagrams. Support each comparison with numbers for air starting at 1 bar and 300 K, and say which comparison matters for real engine design.
outline: η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>; q<sub>out</sub> is the area under the constant-volume line to state 1
case (a): shared 1-2, slopes T/c<sub>v</sub> and T/c<sub>v</sub>, numbers
case (b): shared state 3 and equal heat rejected, numbers

answer.text: Basis: η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>. In all three cycles heat is rejected along a constant-volume line from the end of expansion to state 1, so q<sub>out</sub> is the area under that line on the T-s diagram. On T-s, a constant-volume line has slope T/c<sub>v</sub> and a constant-pressure line T/c<sub>p</sub>, so the constant-volume line is steeper.

(a) Same r and same q<sub>in</sub>. States 1 and 2 are common. To add the same heat (equal areas under the heating lines), the steep constant-volume line of Otto needs less entropy rise than the flatter constant-pressure line of Diesel. The Diesel cycle therefore ends heat addition at a larger entropy, and its rejection line 4′→1 is longer, with more area under it.

Working for the Diesel line: T₃ = 862.1 + 1200/1.005 = 2056.2 K, r<sub>c</sub> = 2056.2/862.1 = 2.385, T₄ = 300 × 2.385<sup>1.4</sup> = 1013.0 K, q<sub>out</sub> = 0.718 × 713.0 = 511.9 kJ/kg. Result (a): η<sub>Otto</sub> > η<sub>Dual</sub> > η<sub>Diesel</sub>.

(b) Same peak pressure and peak temperature. Now state 3 is common, so the expansion 3→4 and the heat rejected 4→1 are the same for all three. The Diesel cycle reaches the peak pressure by compression alone, so it has the highest compression ratio and takes in the most heat; the Otto cycle has the lowest r and the least heat input.
Numbers for a peak of 60 bar and 2000 K:
Result (b): η<sub>Diesel</sub> > η<sub>Dual</sub> > η<sub>Otto</sub>. The same order holds for the same peak pressure and the same heat input.

Mean temperature view: η = 1 − T<sub>m,out</sub>/T<sub>m,in</sub>. In (a) Otto has the highest mean temperature of heat addition; in (b) all three reject at the same mean temperature and Diesel has the highest mean temperature of addition because its heating starts from the hottest state 2.

Evaluation: the cylinder, head and bearings are designed for a maximum pressure, and the materials for a maximum temperature, so comparison (b) is the fair one for engine design. It explains why compression-ignition engines, with their higher compression ratios, are more efficient in practice, even though comparison (a) favours Otto.

bank.q: A cold store in Coimbatore needs 50 kW of cooling at −10 °C, with heat rejected at about 30 °C. Low-pressure steam at 120 °C is available as waste heat from a process. Evaluate a vapour compression system (COP 4.03, from the R-134a cycle between −10 °C and 40 °C) against an ammonia-water absorption system (actual COP 0.55). Compare energy input, heat rejected and the thermodynamic quality of each, and recommend one.
outline: Input power or heat for each
Carnot and ideal absorption COPs as benchmarks
cost of the energy, not just its amount

answer.text: Vapour compression: electric input = 50/4.03 = 12.4 kW; heat rejected at the condenser = 50 + 12.4 = 62.4 kW.
Absorption: generator heat = 50/0.55 = 90.9 kW of steam; heat rejected in the condenser and absorber = 50 + 90.9 = 140.9 kW (pump work of a few hundred watts neglected).

Benchmarks. The compression cycle's limit is the reversed Carnot COP between its evaporator and condenser, 263.15/(313.15 − 263.15) = 5.26, so it reaches 4.03/5.26 = 77%. The absorption limit with T<sub>G</sub> = 393.15 K, T<sub>0</sub> = 303.15 K, T<sub>E</sub> = 263.15 K is

Comparing the inputs fairly: a kilowatt of electricity is worth far more than a kilowatt of 120 °C heat. The most work 90.9 kW of heat at 120 °C could give with the surroundings at 30 °C is 90.9 × (1 − 303.15/393.15) = 20.8 kW. So, by work potential, the absorption system uses 20.8 kW-equivalent against 12.4 kW of electricity for compression: compression is the better machine thermodynamically.

But the steam is waste heat. If it would otherwise be thrown away, the absorption plant's running energy cost is close to zero (only the pump and cooling-water pumps), while the compression plant buys 12.4 kW of electricity: about 12.4 × 24 = 298 kWh a day.

Penalties of absorption: the cooling tower and water flow must handle 140.9 kW instead of 62.4 kW, more than twice as much; the plant is larger and costs more to buy; ammonia needs leak precautions (as it does in large compression cold stores too).
Comparison:

head: Compression
Absorption
rows: near zero if the steam is free

answer.text: Recommendation: choose the absorption system if the waste steam is available whenever cooling is needed and the site can supply the larger cooling-water flow; the saved electricity repays the higher first cost. Choose vapour compression if the steam is intermittent, cooling water is scarce, or the process may later use the steam itself. A common answer is both: absorption for the base load and a compression unit as standby.

bank.q: The Carnot cycle has the highest efficiency between two temperatures, yet power plants use the Brayton, Stirling and Rankine cycles. Using work ratio, mean effective pressure and mean temperature of heat addition, analyse why, with the numbers from this unit's examples.
outline: Carnot limit and its two practical faults
work ratio and MEP of the Carnot example
Brayton: η and work, back work ratio
Rankine: isothermal heat in the dome, mean temperature of heat addition

answer.text: The limit: any engine between T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>L</sub> has η ≤ 1 − T<sub>L</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>. A practical cycle must also give a lot of net work per kg and per litre of machine, and must keep that net work large compared with the losses. Two measures capture this: the work ratio (net work/positive work) and the mean effective pressure.

Carnot with air between 300 K and 900 K (volume ratio 2 during heat addition): η = 66.7%, but w<sub>net</sub> = 119.4 kJ/kg out of 609.8 kJ/kg of positive work, a work ratio of 0.196, and an MEP of only 0.716 bar despite a pressure ratio of 94. A 10% friction loss on the positive work (61.0 kJ/kg) would halve the output. Isothermal heat transfer at engine speed is also impossible.

Brayton (r<sub>p</sub> = 8, 300 to 1200 K): η = 44.8%, lower than Carnot for the same extremes (75%), because heat enters along a rising constant-pressure line from 543 K, not all at 1200 K. Its back work ratio is 0.453, so its work ratio is 0.547, far better than Carnot's, and it is a compact steady-flow machine. The gas-turbine problem example showed the cost of the remaining back work: with 85% and 88% component efficiencies η fell from 48.2% to 33.2%.

Stirling (300 to 900 K, volume ratio 2): the isothermal steps are the same as Carnot's, but the isentropic steps are replaced by constant-volume steps whose heat is stored and returned by the regenerator. With a perfect regenerator η = 66.7%, exactly Carnot, and the constant-volume steps cost no compression work. Without the regenerator η falls to 19.6%; with 80% recovery, 45.0%. The cycle's quality rests on the regenerator.

Rankine (40 bar, 400 °C, 0.1 bar): inside the dome, boiling and condensing are naturally isothermal, so the steam cycle gets Carnot-like heat transfer for free. The pump handles liquid, so w<sub>P</sub> = 4.03 kJ/kg against w<sub>T</sub> = 1070.0 kJ/kg: a work ratio of 0.996. Its efficiency, 35.3%, is below the Carnot value of 52.6% between 400 °C and 45.8 °C because the mean temperature of heat addition is only 493 K; feedwater heating and superheating happen at lower temperatures.
Summary:

Verdict: a practical cycle gives up some ideal efficiency to gain a high work ratio and MEP. Engineers then recover efficiency by raising the mean temperature of heat addition: regeneration and reheat in the Rankine cycle, regenerators and intercooling in gas turbines, and combined gas-steam cycles.

glossary.def: An ideal cycle in which a fixed mass of air, treated as an ideal gas, goes through reversible processes with heat added and rejected from outside.
r = v₁/v₂, the largest volume of the cylinder divided by the clearance volume.
The volume at the end of constant-pressure heat addition divided by the volume at its start (v₃/v₂ in Diesel, v₄/v₃ in Dual).
In the Dual cycle, p₃/p₂ during constant-volume heat addition; in the Brayton cycle, the compressor exit over inlet pressure.
The constant pressure that would do the cycle's net work in one stroke: w<sub>net</sub>/(v₁ − v₂).
Net work divided by the positive (expansion) work of a cycle; low values make a cycle sensitive to losses.
Compressor work divided by turbine work, in a gas turbine or steam plant.
The actual thermal efficiency of an engine divided by its air standard efficiency.
A heat store inside a cycle that takes heat from the working fluid in one process and gives it back in another, as in the Stirling engine.
Self-ignition of part of the fuel-air charge before the flame reaches it, which limits the compression ratio of petrol engines.
Steam needed per kWh of net work, 3600/w<sub>net</sub> kg/kWh.
The mass of vapour divided by the total mass of a wet steam mixture.
Heating steam again at an intermediate pressure between two turbine stages, to keep the exhaust drier.
A mixing chamber in which bled steam mixes with feedwater at the bleed pressure; it needs a pump after it.
A shell-and-tube exchanger in which bled steam heats feedwater without mixing.
The open feedwater heater of a large plant, which also removes dissolved gases from the water.
q<sub>in</sub> divided by the entropy rise during heat addition; the higher it is, the higher the cycle efficiency.
Useful heat moved divided by the energy input: cooling over work for a refrigerator, heating over work for a heat pump.
A cooling rate of 211 kJ/min, or 3.517 kW.
Heat taken from the cold space per kg of refrigerant, h₁ − h₄.
An irreversible pressure drop through a valve at constant enthalpy.
Cooling the condensed liquid below its saturation temperature before the expansion valve.
The vessel of an absorption plant where refrigerant vapour dissolves in the absorbent, releasing heat.
The vessel where heat drives the refrigerant out of the strong solution at high pressure.
The part above the generator of an ammonia-water plant that condenses water vapour out of the ammonia vapour.
